opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so one of the big bottlenecks in reinforcement learning has always been the environments themselves. If you want a truly generalist agent, you need it to train on a huge diversity of worlds, and historically every one of those had to be hand-built: someone designs the game, writes the physics, defines the action space. That just doesn't scale to the breadth of experience we think a general agent needs.

What's exciting about Genie is that it flips that around. Instead of hand-engineering environments, we learn them from data, specifically from large amounts of internet video, much of it 2D platformer gameplay. The model learns, without any action labels, a latent action space: a small set of discrete controls that explain how one frame transitions to the next. Combined with a video tokenizer and a dynamics model, you end up with something you can prompt with an image, even a sketch or a photo, and then actually *play*, stepping it forward frame by frame with those latent actions.

So the vision is that this becomes a kind of generator of endless, controllable worlds. Rather than being limited to a fixed suite of games, you could in principle create new environments on demand, and that opens the door to open-ended learning, where agents keep encountering novel situations.

We also showed early signs that the latent actions are meaningful beyond games. We trained a version on robotics video and found it learned consistent actions there too. And we did some experiments where the latent action model could be used to label unseen videos, which you could then use for imitation learning with only a small amount of real action data.

Now, I want to be honest that it's early. The frame rate is low, the generations can drift or hallucinate over long horizons, and there's a lot of work left before this is a drop-in training ground for agents. But I see it as a first step toward foundation world models, where the environment itself is something we can scale with data and compute, the same way we've scaled language and vision models.

r001.rationale: The response says environments were historically hand-built and that this approach “doesn't scale” to the diversity a generalist agent needs.

r002.rationale: It describes Genie as a generator of “endless, controllable worlds” that can create new environments on demand for open-ended learning.

r003.rationale: The response says the worlds can be played by stepping them forward with latent actions, but does not clearly state that this interaction happens without placing the agent in the environment itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the thing that motivated the work in the first place. If you think about where the big successes in reinforcement learning have come from, a lot of them have been in settings where you have a simulator you can run essentially forever, like Atari or Go or physics engines. But if we want agents that are truly general, that can act in lots of different environments and ideally transfer to the real world, we hit a bottleneck pretty quickly. Somebody has to build each of those environments by hand, and that doesn't scale. You can't hand-code every room, every game, every physical scenario you'd want an agent to experience.

So the idea behind Genie was to ask whether we could learn the environment instead. There's an enormous amount of video on the internet of people playing games, and of people doing things in the world. That data has structure in it. It shows you how things move, what happens when a character jumps or walks into a wall, how scenes evolve over time. The question was whether a model could absorb that and become a kind of generative interactive environment, where you can give it a single image, or even a sketch, and then step through it frame by frame with actions.

The piece that I think is most interesting for the RL angle is that we trained it without any action labels. The videos we used don't come with annotations saying "the player pressed left here." Genie learns a latent action space on its own, just from watching how frames change. And what we found is that those latent actions end up being fairly consistent across different scenes, so the same latent action tends to mean something like "move right" whether you're in a cartoon world or a photograph.

That matters for generalist agents in a couple of ways. First, it means you can in principle generate an unbounded number of environments, so the diversity problem becomes much more tractable. Second, because the latent actions are shared, an agent trained in these generated worlds has a foundation it can carry across them. We did some early experiments showing that the latent actions learned from one set of videos can be used to imitate behavior in an unseen environment. It's still very early, and the model has real limitations around things like consistency over long horizons and the frame rate, but to me it points toward a future where the environment itself is something you train rather than something you build.

r001.rationale: The response says each environment would have to be built by hand and that this does not scale to general agents.

r002.rationale: It describes generating an “unbounded number of environments” as a motivation for learning the environment with Genie.

r003.rationale: It describes Genie as a generative interactive environment that can be stepped through with actions, and says agents can train in generated worlds, conveying interaction through the model rather than direct placement in a real environment.

astra-6.text:
One of the big challenges with training generalist reinforcement learning agents is having enough diversity in the environments they interact with. If you have to build every environment by hand, that becomes a real bottleneck. With Genie, the idea is to learn from video how to generate environments that an agent can actually interact with, rather than just generating a video that it watches.

So you could imagine starting from an image or a sketch and creating a world where an agent can take actions and see what happens. That opens up the possibility of training across a much broader range of situations. The exciting question is whether that diversity helps agents learn skills that transfer to environments they haven’t seen before. Generating an interactive world is one piece; making those worlds useful for learning and generalization is the next.

r001.rationale: It says hand-building every environment becomes a bottleneck for providing the diversity generalist agents need.

r002.rationale: It describes a broader range of training situations, but does not identify an unlimited source of environments as a motivation.

r003.rationale: It says agents can interact with generated worlds, but does not explain that this interactivity is provided without placing the agent in the environment itself.

sol-6.1.text:
One of the big challenges for generalist reinforcement learning is having a sufficiently diverse set of environments. If you want an agent to learn lots of different skills, you need worlds where it can practice those skills, and building each of those worlds by hand is difficult to scale.

With Genie, the idea is to learn an interactive environment from video. Instead of only generating a video that you watch, you can take actions and influence what happens next. That opens up the possibility of generating a much broader range of environments for agents to learn in.

The particularly interesting part is that the training videos don’t need action labels. Genie learns a latent action space that lets you control the environments it generates. So you can imagine using video as a source of experience for building training worlds, rather than needing someone to explicitly program every environment. It’s a step toward that broader goal, though there’s still work to do to make those worlds sufficiently reliable and diverse for generalist agents.

r001.rationale: It says building each training world by hand is difficult to scale for agents that need many skills.

r002.rationale: It describes a broader range of environments, but does not identify an unlimited source of training environments as a motivation.

r003.rationale: It explains that agents can take actions in generated environments, but does not say this provides interactivity without placing the agent in the environment itself.
